title: Habakkuk 1:5–11
context: The LORD answers Habakkuk’s complaint: “Look among the nations, watch, and wonder marvelously,” for he is doing a work that would not be believed even if told (1:5). He is raising up the Chaldeans, a “bitter and hasty nation,” feared, laws unto themselves, swift and fierce, scoffing at kings and strongholds (1:6–10). Yet the oracle ends with a verdict: “They are indeed guilty, whose strength is their god” (1:11). The LORD claims to raise up a violent nation and still holds it guilty. For how the two traditions describe God’s use of hostile agents while remaining just and not the author of sin, see the Judges 9:23 box, which applies here and is not restated. Many date this oracle to the years when Babylon rose to dominance in the late seventh century BC, perhaps around 605 BC, but the text gives no date and the timing is held with caution. Paul cites 1:5 as a warning in Acts 13:41, a later use named here without merging it with the original setting. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that the LORD rules the nations, that his instruments remain responsible for their deeds, and that his answer exceeds what his people expect.

verses.text: “Look among the nations, watch, and wonder marvelously; for I am working a work in your days which you will not believe though it is told you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Look among the nations, watch, and wonder marvelously.” The LORD answers with a work “which you will not believe though it is told you.” Arminian readers see God responding to the prophet’s prayer, though not as expected, and hear a summons to look beyond Judah to what he is doing in history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the LORD declares his work in advance, showing that the coming events are his doing, however unbelievable. Shared ground: both traditions note that Paul applies this verse as a warning to his hearers in Acts 13:41, read that use alongside the original setting without merging the two, and see God at work beyond what his people expect.

verses.text: For, behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation who march through the width of the earth, to possess dwelling places that are not theirs.
verses.arminianNotes: “For, behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans.” Arminian readers generally describe God directing a nation already bent on conquest toward his purposes of judgment, without making him the author of its cruelty; the Chaldeans’ ambitions are their own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers generally hold that God ordains and governs the rise of Babylon, so that even a “bitter and hasty nation” serves his purpose while remaining guilty. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that the LORD rules over the nations and is not the author of sin.

verses.text: They are feared and dreaded. Their judgment and their dignity proceed from themselves.
verses.arminianNotes: “They are feared and dreaded. Their judgment and their dignity proceed from themselves.” Arminian readers see a nation that recognizes no authority beyond itself, a self-made law that sets the stage for its own judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the irony: the nation thinks its authority proceeds from itself, yet verse 6 has declared that the LORD raised it up. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as exposing the pride of empire, and both see the claim to self-derived authority as the very thing for which the Chaldeans will be held to account in the woes of chapter 2.

verses.text: Their horses also are swifter than leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves. Their horsemen press proudly on. Yes, their horsemen come from afar. They fly as an eagle that hurries to devour.
verses.arminianNotes: “Their horses also are swifter than leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves.” Arminian readers note the terrifying speed and ferocity, which underline how serious the coming judgment is and how urgently Judah needed to heed earlier warnings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the images of leopard, wolf, and eagle as heightening the dread of an instrument God wields, whose power no human stronghold can resist. Shared ground: both traditions read the animal imagery as poetry of overwhelming military might, and both see it as a description of the instrument rather than a commendation of its violence.

verses.text: All of them come for violence. Their hordes face forward. They gather prisoners like sand.
verses.arminianNotes: “All of them come for violence.” Arminian readers note the irony: Habakkuk cried out about violence in Judah (1:2–3), and the answer is a more violent nation, whose violence is its own choice and will be judged in turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD answering violence with judgment through violent agents, a sobering reminder that his ways exceed human expectation. Shared ground: both traditions read “They gather prisoners like sand” as a picture of mass deportation, and both note that the word “violence” ties the LORD’s answer directly back to the prophet’s complaint.

verses.text: Yes, they scoff at kings, and princes are a derision to them. They laugh at every stronghold, for they build up an earthen ramp and take it.
verses.arminianNotes: “Yes, they scoff at kings, and princes are a derision to them.” Arminian readers see a nation that mocks every human power and defense, a pride that will be turned back on itself in the woes of chapter 2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that no stronghold can stand against the instrument God has raised up, since “they build up an earthen ramp and take it.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing siege warfare and contempt for rulers, and both see the scoffing as a mark of arrogance that the LORD will judge in his time.

verses.text: Then they sweep by like the wind and go on. They are indeed guilty, whose strength is their god.”
verses.arminianNotes: “They are indeed guilty, whose strength is their god.” Arminian readers stress the decisive point: though used by God, the Chaldeans are guilty for their own choices, above all for making their strength their god.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that God’s governing use of Babylon does not make Babylon innocent; idolatry of power is its own sin, for which it answers. Shared ground: both traditions hold together God’s rule over the nations and the full guilt of his instruments, and both see self-worship as the root sin here.
